analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal court's approval before a special counsel can be fired.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in September 2017, it sat without action until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Attorney General from firing a special counsel on his own. Instead, any removal would require filing a court action, notice to Congress, and a federal court order finding misconduct, dereliction of duty, incapacity, conflict of interest, or other good cause. It was written at a time when a special counsel was investigating matters touching the White House, and its effect would have been to keep that investigation beyond the reach of a single appointee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens' interest in having senior officials investigated independently: a special counsel could not be removed by the one cabinet officer the President controls, so an investigation could not be ended or redirected by firing the investigator. It also protects any special counsel directly, since firing them would require a court to find cause on the record.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone relying on an independent prosecutor

how_it_helps.text: A special counsel, or any similarly independent official appointed by the Attorney General, could be removed only after the Attorney General files an action in federal district court in Washington and simultaneously notifies the House and Senate Judiciary Committees.
Removal requires a court order finding misconduct, dereliction of duty, incapacity, conflict of interest, or other good cause, with appeals going straight to the Supreme Court.

analysis.who_pays: A President and Attorney General lose the power to remove a special counsel at will; the executive branch gains a judicial check on one of its personnel decisions, and removal of a badly performing prosecutor becomes slower and public.
analysis.who_pays_short: A President's removal power over investigators

drawbacks.text: Conditioning the removal of an executive-branch officer on a court order raises a real separation-of-powers question: under the Constitution's assignment of executive power to the President, courts have held that officials exercising executive authority generally must be removable by the President or an executive supervisor, and this bill would set that rule aside for special counsels.

The same protection cuts both ways: a conflicted or underperforming special counsel could not be replaced without the Attorney General first prevailing in a court case, so problems inside an investigation would be slower to fix and removal would become a public legal fight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is narrow and targeted: it leaves removal for genuine cause possible but takes away the option of firing an investigator without a public, court-reviewed justification. The cost is slower removal and a genuine constitutional dispute over whether Congress can put a judge between the President and a subordinate. For a safeguard aimed at keeping investigations of the powerful honest, the trade is a reasonable one, though the constitutional challenge would likely have been litigated immediately had it passed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held a hearing but never voted to send it to the Senate floor, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican, introduced the bill on August 3, 2017, joined by three Democratic cosponsors, Senators Booker, Whitehouse, and Blumenthal.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
The committee held a hearing on September 26, 2017, its only action beyond referral.
The bill never received a vote in committee or on the Senate floor and died at the end of the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The President and Attorney General kept the power to remove a special counsel without a court's approval, and no protections like these ever took effect. Readers can judge for themselves what that means about whose interests the Senate chose to protect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: A President's power to fire investigators stayed untouched

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small support was genuinely bipartisan — a Republican sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors — but with only four senators behind it and no votes ever taken, the record shows no party split to measure.

industries.industry: Incumbent officials and the executive branch's removal power
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the President and Attorney General of the power to fire a special counsel at will, requiring a public court finding of cause instead. The interest protected by the bill's absence is the officeholders' own discretion over who investigates them.
